opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to accept that people leaving is normal. Talented people have their own trajectories. Someone might want to start a company, try a different research direction, or just need a change of environment. If an organization treats every departure as a betrayal or a crisis, that's actually a sign something is unhealthy.

A healthy organization shouldn't depend too much on any single person. If one person leaving makes a whole project collapse, the knowledge was never really shared. The code, the infrastructure, the documentation, and the reasoning behind decisions should live in the system, not just in someone's head. That matters a lot in engineering. If you build good tooling and good processes, the next person can pick things up and keep going.

Second, I think it's important to part on good terms. The community is small, especially in AI. The person who leaves today might collaborate with you, come back, or recommend great people to you later. So being respectful, being honest about why someone is leaving, and not burning bridges is just the right long-term strategy.

Third, a departure is a signal you should actually listen to. If many strong people are leaving for similar reasons, maybe they feel they don't have ownership, or the direction isn't clear, or the culture has changed. Leadership should treat that as feedback, not just as attrition numbers.

And finally, the organization should keep creating space for the people who stay. When someone senior leaves, that's often an opportunity for others to step up and take on more responsibility. If you handle it well, the team can come out of it stronger. So to me, it's less about preventing people from leaving and more about making the place somewhere people *want* to stay, and making sure it keeps working well when they don't.

r001.rationale: The response says the organization should not depend on any single person and that shared knowledge and processes should let the next person continue the work, conveying replaceability.

r002.rationale: It mentions the next person picking up work and existing team members stepping up, but does not identify continuously cultivating newcomers as a way to sustain the organization.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, partly because I've been on both sides of it. I've left teams, and I've watched people I really valued leave teams I was on.

The first thing I'd say is that a healthy organization treats departures as normal, not as betrayal. People grow, their interests shift, their lives change. If you've hired ambitious, curious people, some of them will eventually want to do something you can't offer. That's not a failure of the organization. In a way it's a sign the hiring worked.

The second thing is how you handle the moment itself. The instinct for a lot of managers is to get defensive, or to immediately start damage control, or to quietly cut the person out of things during their notice period. I think that's a mistake. How you treat someone on their way out is watched very closely by everyone who's staying. If you're gracious, if you thank them publicly, if you let them finish strong and hand things off properly, the people remaining learn that this is a place where they'll be respected even when they're no longer useful to you. If you're petty about it, they learn the opposite, and they start planning their own exits more carefully.

The third thing is the engineering side, which I care about because of my background. Departures are a stress test for how well knowledge is shared. If one person leaving means a whole system becomes a black box, the problem wasn't that the person left. The problem was that you let one person become a single point of failure. So I'd actually use departures as a diagnostic. Every time someone leaves, ask honestly: what did we only know because of them? And then fix that structurally, through documentation, pairing, rotation, whatever works, rather than just hoping the next person stays forever.

And finally, I'd say keep the door open. Some of the best relationships I have are with former colleagues. They become collaborators, they send people your way, sometimes they come back. Treating a departure as the end of a relationship instead of a change in it is just leaving value on the table.

So in short: don't take it personally, be generous in the moment, learn from what it reveals, and stay in touch.

r001.rationale: The response says a departure should not leave a system as a black box or make someone a single point of failure, but it does not state that everyone should be replaceable.

r002.rationale: It recommends documentation, pairing, and rotation to share knowledge, but does not identify continuously cultivating newcomers as a way to sustain operations through departures.

astra-6.text:
I think a healthy organization should be able to celebrate someone’s contribution even when they decide to leave. Of course, losing a talented person can be painful. But you can be disappointed and still support their next step.

It’s also an opportunity to listen. Were they looking for growth you couldn’t offer? Was there something in the culture that made it difficult for them to stay? You don’t have to assume every departure means something is wrong, but you should be willing to learn.

And internally, you need to take care of the people who remain—make the transition clear, share knowledge, and avoid simply dropping all the work on them. To me, the goal isn’t to build an organization that nobody ever leaves. It’s to build one where people do meaningful work, grow, and can leave with mutual respect.

r001.rationale: The response supports people leaving and managing transitions, but does not state that everyone should be replaceable.

r002.rationale: It mentions sharing knowledge and supporting remaining staff, but does not identify continuously cultivating newcomers as a way to sustain the organization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a healthy organization should be able to celebrate someone’s contribution and support their next step, even when it’s hard to lose them. You can want someone to stay without making them feel guilty for leaving.

It’s also a chance to listen. What made them want to move on? Is there something the organization needs to improve, or do they simply want an experience you can’t offer? Those are different situations.

And ideally, the team has shared knowledge and developed people so that one departure doesn’t become a crisis. To me, success includes helping people grow—even when that growth eventually takes them somewhere else.

r001.rationale: The response says shared knowledge and developed people can prevent one departure from becoming a crisis, but does not state that everyone should be replaceable.

r002.rationale: It mentions developing people and sharing knowledge, but does not identify continuously cultivating newcomers as a way to maintain organizational functioning after departures.
